query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with an optimized composition featuring increased Cr content and complementary oxide-forming elements (such as Ti or Al) will form an in-situ, continuous protective oxide/spinel layer under high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions, resulting in superior degradation resistance compared to conventional structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional structural alloys that exhibit rapid degradation under the combined stresses of elevated temperature, wear, and corrosive environments.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an HEA composition with increased Cr along with other oxide-formers (e.g., Ti or Al) to control phase formation and promote the formation of a protective oxide layer.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature combined with mechanical wear (tribological stress) and corrosive exposure, typical of extreme environmental applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous and adherent oxide or spinel layer that serves as a barrier against further oxidation and mechanical wear.
generation.mechanism: The increased Cr and complementary elements facilitate the in-situ formation of a stable protective oxide/spinel layer during service. This layer effectively slows down oxidation and limits corrosive and mechanical degradation, thereby enhancing tribo-corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized HEA will exhibit reduced weight gain (or mass loss), lower friction coefficients, and improved overall microstructural stability under tested high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions relative to conventional alloys.
generation.baseline: Standard structural alloys lacking optimized oxide-forming element content, which degrade rapidly under combined high temperature, wear, and corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The enhanced performance is expected under dynamic high-temperature tribo-corrosion conditions; outcomes may vary if the environmental parameters (such as temperature, wear load, and corrosive medium composition) deviate significantly from the tested regime.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise optimal levels of Cr and complementary elements needed, as well as the kinetics of the protective layer formation under varying service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of conventional alloys and one set of the proposed optimized HEA (with increased Cr and selected oxide-forming elements). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tribo-corrosion testing that simulates combined wear and corrosive exposure. Monitor the formation of oxide layers using in situ techniques (e.g., XRD) and complement these with weight change measurements, friction tests, and microstructural characterization over time.
measurements: Weight change (gain or loss) as an indicator of oxidation/corrosion behavior
Coefficient of friction during wear tests
Thickness and continuity of the protective oxide/spinel layer (via microscopy and XRD)
Phase composition and microstructure analysis before and after corrosion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized HEA does not show statistically significant improvements in tribo-corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight change, friction levels, and lack of protective oxide formation) compared to the conventional alloys under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by intervening on the material composition—specifically by tailoring high-entropy alloy formulations to enhance the formation of protective oxide films and phase stability. frame.understanding: There is a need to understand and design alloy compositions that incorporate elements which promote the formation of stable, protective oxide layers (or passive films) and also benefit from the inherent high strength and thermal stability of HEAs. This understanding is crucial for tailoring the alloy’s microstructure to impede both mechanical wear and corrosion processes.

decision.trend: Several studies have progressively tailored HEA microstructures to enhance performance under extreme environments. Early works focused on establishing phase stability and microstructural changes under irradiation or thermal-mechanical conditions, while later studies (e.g., PMC7515071) concentrated on the wear behavior of HEAs at elevated temperatures. These works revealed that specific multiphase microstructures can trigger the in situ formation of protective phases, such as spinels, which reduce wear when tested at high temperatures. However, while these investigations improved wear resistance by controlling precipitate formation and phase distribution, the simultaneous mitigation of both wear and corrosive degradation—the hallmark of tribo‐corrosion—remains unaddressed.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge is to design an HEA that, under the dynamic conditions of high temperature and tribological stress, forms a stable and continuous protective oxide or spinel layer that can effectively counter both mechanical wear and corrosive attack. Current studies either optimize for mechanical robustness or oxidation/corrosion resistance separately, leaving a gap in combined tribo‐corrosion performance.
decision.lever: optimized Cr (and complementary oxide-forming elements, e.g., Ti or Al) content
decision.why: Following the observed trend where controlled compositional adjustments lead to the formation of beneficial precipitates and protective phases (as in the formation of a spinel phase at elevated temperatures in PMC7515071), the most plausible next step is to fine‐tune the alloy composition. By increasing Cr content (along with other carefully selected oxide formers), the alloy can be engineered to form a continuous, adherent protective oxide/spinel layer during service, thereby enhancing the tribo‐corrosion resistance. This approach directly addresses the need for improved material performance under the combined stresses of high temperature, wear, and corrosive environments.
